source.title: Computational Superposition in a Toy Model of the U-AND Problem

record.tranche_reason: The post reports results for computational superposition in a toy U-AND task, but does not test whether neurons in trained networks have unrelated input meanings. It explicitly distinguishes computational superposition from neuron polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The post's experiments concern a toy model learning reusable computations of Boolean AND pairs, not neuron responses to unrelated natural inputs or the prevalence of polysemantic neurons. Its discussion of XOR and polysemanticity is framing, not a direct measurement of the claim versions. Rows below record the related computational-superposition findings under versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The post trains a toy two-layer ReLU model on synthetic sparse Boolean inputs (Universal-AND) and analyses the dense 'binary weighted' circuit it learns. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs in vision or language models. It never measures the share of polysemantic neurons, or how that share varies with architecture or measurement. Its 'neurons' read every input by construction of the learned solution. The post frames this as computational superposition, explicitly distinct from neuron polysemanticity. So its results bear on a related construct, not on any version as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes that a toy model learns a dense binary-weighted circuit for U-AND rather than the sparse CiS construction, giving empirical support to computation in superposition. They argue weight decay biases training toward dense circuits, and that this explains why XOR is often linearly readable. Dense circuits challenge interpretability methods that assume sparse circuits. Finding such circuitry in a real LLM remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains a toy U-AND model and analyzes its learned circuits; it does not apply the original neuron-interpretability method.
record.method_sensitivity: Input sparsity changes the learned pattern: higher sparsity can yield degenerate solutions, and mixed sparsity yields less neat binary weights.

fits_no_version.finding: In the toy U-AND task the learned circuit is dense: every neuron reads every input with one of two weight values. Pairwise ANDs are read out linearly from all neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained toy networks solve Boolean AND computation with dense circuits in which each neuron participates in many unrelated computations (computational superposition).

fits_no_version.finding: At higher input sparsity (s≥10, m=100, d≤m) the model prefers degenerate solutions: pure-additive circuits, or leaving the first-layer weights unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The learned computational-superposition solution depends on input sparsity and hidden width.

fits_no_version.finding: Random or frozen compute-layer weights with a fitted readout give a similar readout pattern and similar loss, worse by a constant factor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy Boolean tasks, random mixing of sparse inputs followed by ReLU already supports linear readout of arbitrary Boolean functions.

fits_no_version.finding: Footnote: even at d=m² the author found no naive 1:1 neuron:output solution, attributing the dense mixed circuit to weight decay. The post also states that mixing inputs helps computation without narrow-dimension pressure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization can favour neurons that mix many unrelated inputs even when there are enough neurons for one per output. This is related to V4 but concerns computation, not measured neuron polysemanticity.

record.problems: The evidence is from a toy model and synthetic task, which the author says is not very representative of real situations. The post reports some outcomes qualitatively without numerical losses or frequencies; it also says further parameter sweeps and scaling-law work are needed.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported experiment was included because the post's remaining discussion is theoretical analysis, interpretation, or limitations rather than a separately reported empirical result bearing on the claim's subject.

untested.parts: No vision models or image inputs.
No language models; no prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons by layer.
No test that neuron polysemanticity in trained networks is caused by feature packing. The toy studies computation reuse.
No measurement of neuron polysemanticity arising when capacity suffices. Only a footnote remark at d=m² in a toy computation task.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron share across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

missing.what: Observation that at d=m² (enough neurons for every AND output) the model still learned no 1:1 neuron:output strategy. The author attributes the dense mixed circuit to weight decay. It is qualitative only and has no row.
missing.locator: Footnote to Conclusion (final footnote); 'Is This Just Feature Superposition?' takeaways
missing.versions: none (related to V4, but measures computational mixing, not neuron polysemanticity)

missing.what: Variant forcing weights to the binary pattern with smoothing: it converged slower than training the full matrix. No row records it.

Analytic variance comparison: the dense circuit is O(s²/d) vs the sparse CiS construction's O(s·log²m/√d). The dense circuit is preferred when s grows slower than √d/log²m. This is theory, not a measurement.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses gate is kept. The post explicitly separates computational superposition from neuron polysemanticity, and its only real-network relevance is framing. The closest point of contact is V4, via the d=m² footnote and the weight-decay argument. That evidence is a qualitative remark in a synthetic computation task with no polysemanticity measure, so no verdict is given. The post is a non-peer-reviewed LessWrong post; code is released.

versions.untested_parts: No vision models or image inputs tested.
No language models, tokens, or contexts tested.
The post studies computational superposition in a toy task, not whether superposition causes neurons to respond to unrelated features.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron prevalence across activations, architectures, or regularization, or of its relation to performance.
No investigation of whether apparent mixed neuron responses share a coherent feature.
No comparison of neuron-polysemanticity measures or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: toy two-layer model (m=100, d=1000, s=3 is the typical setting)
rows.operation_detail: Trained a ReLU compute layer and linear readout on synthetic sparse Boolean inputs to predict every pairwise AND.

conditions.value: RMS with up-weighting to equalize expected contribution of 0∧0, 1∧0, and 1∧1 cases

rows.measure: Whether the model learns a solution to the U-AND task and the qualitative pattern of its learned weights
rows.value: At low s, the model finds solutions capable of solving U-AND, including at extremely low d; learned weights generally trend toward a dense binary-weighted pattern.
rows.note: This is a result about reusable computation in the toy task, not about whether an individual neuron has one coherent meaning.

rows.subject: toy two-layer model (m=100)
rows.operation_detail: Trained the model on the U-AND task at higher input sparsity.
rows.value: The model starts to prefer degenerate solutions, including pure-additive circuits roughly corresponding to zᵢₘ₊ⱼ=0.4(vᵢ+vⱼ), or failure to update the first-layer weights with reliance on readout weights.
rows.note: The post reports these as alternative degenerate outcomes; it does not quantify their frequency.
rows.check: State 'partial' has no referent: the row is not linked to any version. The text reports the degenerate solutions qualitatively, with no frequency or loss. The value '0.4' is a coefficient of the additive circuit, not an outcome measure.

rows.subject: same toy model with randomized compute-layer weights
rows.stage_stated: readout matrix optimized; compute-layer weights randomized
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated randomized compute weights while optimizing only the readout matrix.
rows.baseline: trained model loss; exact value not stated
rows.value: Similar loss, but worse by a constant factor.
rows.note: The post does not give the constant factor or numerical loss.
rows.check: State 'partial' is not meaningful for an unlinked row. The text says randomized weights with an optimized readout give similar loss, 'worse by a constant factor'. No number is given.
